blocks.source: # CHAPTER 4  GRAPHS
blocks.translation: # 第 4 章　图像

blocks.source: Mention the real numbers to a mathematician and the image of a straight line will probably form in her mind, quite involuntarily. And most likely she will neither banish nor too eagerly embrace this mental picture of the real numbers. “Geometric intuition” will allow her to interpret statements about numbers in terms of this picture, and may even suggest methods of proving them. Although the properties of the real numbers which were studied in Part I are not greatly illuminated by a geometric picture, such an interpretation will be a great aid in Part II.
blocks.translation: 向一位数学家提起实数，她脑海中很可能会不由自主地浮现出一条直线。她大概既不会排斥这个实数的心象，也不会过分热衷于它。“几何直觉”使她能够借助这幅图景解释关于数的陈述，甚至可能启发证明的方法。虽然几何图景对第一部分所研究的实数性质帮助不大，但这种解释将在第二部分中大有用处。

blocks.source: You are probably already familiar with the conventional method of considering the straight line as a picture of the real numbers, i.e., of associating to each real number a point on a line. To do this (Figure 1) we pick, arbitrarily, a point which we label 0, and a point to the right, which we label 1. The point twice as far to the right is labeled 2, the point the same distance from 0 to 1, but to the left of 0, is labeled $-1$, etc. With this arrangement, if $a<b$, then the point corresponding to $a$ lies to the left of the point corresponding to $b$. We can also draw rational numbers, such as $\frac12$, in the obvious way. It is usually taken for granted that the irrational numbers also somehow fit into this scheme, so that every real number can be drawn as a point on the line. We will not make too much fuss about justifying this assumption, since this method of “drawing” numbers is intended solely as a method of picturing certain abstract ideas, and our proofs will never rely on these pictures (although we will frequently use a picture to suggest or help explain a proof). Because this geometric picture plays such a prominent, albeit inessential role, geometric terminology is frequently employed when speaking of numbers—thus a number is sometimes called a *point*, and $\mathbf R$ is often called the *real line*.
blocks.translation: 你大概已经熟悉把直线看成实数图景的通常方法，也就是给每个实数对应直线上的一个点。为此（图 1），任取一点标为 0，再取它右边的一点标为 1。向右距离为两倍的点标为 2；在 0 左边、到 0 的距离等于 0 到 1 的距离的点标为 $-1$，依此类推。按照这种安排，如果 $a<b$，那么 $a$ 对应的点就在 $b$ 对应的点左边。我们还可以用显而易见的方法画出有理数，例如 $\frac12$。通常，人们理所当然地认为，无理数也能以某种方式纳入这一安排，从而每个实数都能画成直线上的一个点。我们不打算过分纠缠这一假设的论证，因为这种“画”数的方法，只是用来形象地表示某些抽象观念，我们的证明绝不依赖这些图画（虽然经常借助图画启发或解释证明）。由于这幅几何图景虽然并非必需，却扮演着如此突出的角色，人们谈论数时常使用几何术语：例如，有时把一个数称为一个*点*，也常把 $\mathbf R$ 称为*实直线*。

blocks.source: The number $|a-b|$ has a simple interpretation in terms of this geometric picture: it is the *distance* between $a$ and $b$, the length of the line segment which has $a$ as one end point and $b$ as the other. This means, to choose an example whose frequent occurrence justifies special consideration, that the set of numbers $x$ which satisfy $|x-a|<\varepsilon$ may be pictured as the collection of points whose distance from $a$ is less than $\varepsilon$. This set of points is the “interval” from $a-\varepsilon$ to $a+\varepsilon$, which may also be described as the points corresponding to numbers $x$ with $a-\varepsilon<x<a+\varepsilon$ (Figure 2).
blocks.translation: 在这幅几何图景中，数 $|a-b|$ 有一个简单的解释：它是 $a$ 与 $b$ 之间的*距离*，即以 $a$ 和 $b$ 为两个端点的线段的长度。举一个因频繁出现而值得特别讨论的例子：满足 $|x-a|<\varepsilon$ 的数 $x$ 的集合，可以画成到 $a$ 的距离小于 $\varepsilon$ 的点的集合。这个点集就是从 $a-\varepsilon$ 到 $a+\varepsilon$ 的“区间”，也可描述为满足 $a-\varepsilon<x<a+\varepsilon$ 的数 $x$ 所对应的点（图 2）。

blocks.source: Sets of numbers which correspond to intervals arise so frequently that it is desirable to have special names for them. The set $\{x:a<x<b\}$ is denoted by $(a,b)$ and called the **open interval** from $a$ to $b$. This notation naturally creates some ambiguity, since $(a,b)$ is also used to denote a pair of numbers, but in context it is always clear (or can easily be made clear) whether one is talking about a pair or an interval. Note that if $a\ge b$, then $(a,b)=\varnothing$, the set with no elements; in prac-
blocks.translation: 对应于区间的数集出现得如此频繁，以至于有必要给它们专门的名称。集合 $\{x:a<x<b\}$ 记作 $(a,b)$，称为从 $a$ 到 $b$ 的**开区间**。这个记号自然会产生一些歧义，因为 $(a,b)$ 也用于表示一个数对；但根据上下文，总能清楚地知道（或者很容易澄清）所谈的是数对还是区间。注意，如果 $a\ge b$，那么 $(a,b)=\varnothing$，即不含任何元素的集合；不过在实际

blocks.source: tice, however, it is almost always assumed (explicitly if one has been careful, and implicitly otherwise), that whenever an interval $(a,b)$ is mentioned, the number $a$ is less than $b$.
blocks.translation: 使用中，几乎总是假定：一旦提到区间 $(a,b)$，数 $a$ 就小于 $b$（仔细的人会明确说明，否则便是默认）。

blocks.source: The set $\{x:a\le x\le b\}$ is denoted by $[a,b]$ and is called the **closed interval** from $a$ to $b$. This symbol is usually reserved for the case $a<b$, but it is sometimes used for $a=b$, also. The usual pictures for the intervals $(a,b)$ and $[a,b]$ are shown in Figure 3; since no reasonably accurate picture could ever indicate the difference between the two intervals, various conventions have been adopted. Figure 3 also shows certain “infinite” intervals. The set $\{x:x>a\}$ is denoted by $(a,\infty)$, while the set $\{x:x\ge a\}$ is denoted by $[a,\infty)$; the sets $(-\infty,a)$ and $(-\infty,a]$ are defined similarly. At this point a standard warning must be issued: the symbols $\infty$ and $-\infty$, though usually read “infinity” and “minus infinity,” are *purely suggestive*; there is no number “$\infty$” which satisfies $\infty\ge a$ for all numbers $a$. While the symbols $\infty$ and $-\infty$ will appear in many contexts, it is always necessary to define these uses in ways that refer only to numbers. The set $\mathbf R$ of all real numbers is also considered to be an “interval,” and is sometimes denoted by $(-\infty,\infty)$.
blocks.translation: 集合 $\{x:a\le x\le b\}$ 记作 $[a,b]$，称为从 $a$ 到 $b$ 的**闭区间**。这个符号通常只用于 $a<b$ 的情形，但有时也用于 $a=b$。图 3 给出了区间 $(a,b)$ 和 $[a,b]$ 的常用画法；由于任何足够准确的图画都无法真正表示这两个区间的区别，人们便采用了各种约定。图 3 还给出了某些“无限”区间。集合 $\{x:x>a\}$ 记作 $(a,\infty)$，集合 $\{x:x\ge a\}$ 记作 $[a,\infty)$；集合 $(-\infty,a)$ 和 $(-\infty,a]$ 的定义类似。这里必须给出一个标准的提醒：符号 $\infty$ 和 $-\infty$ 虽通常读作“无穷大”和“负无穷大”，却*纯粹起提示作用*；并不存在一个数“$\infty$”，使它对所有数 $a$ 都满足 $\infty\ge a$。符号 $\infty$ 和 $-\infty$ 会在许多场合出现，但每一次使用，都必须仅用涉及数的方式来定义。所有实数的集合 $\mathbf R$ 也被看作一个“区间”，有时记作 $(-\infty,\infty)$。

blocks.source: Of even greater interest to us than the method of drawing numbers is a method of drawing pairs of numbers. This procedure, probably also familiar to you, requires a “coordinate system,” two straight lines intersecting at right angles. To distinguish these straight lines, we call one the *horizontal axis*, and one the *vertical axis*. (More prosaic terminology, such as the “first” and “second” axes, is probably preferable from a logical point of view, but most people hold their books, or at least their blackboards, in the same way, so that “horizontal” and “vertical” are more descriptive.) Each of the two axes could be labeled with real numbers, but we can also label points on the horizontal axis with pairs $(a,0)$ and points on the vertical axis with pairs $(0,b)$, so that the intersection of the two axes, the “origin” of the coordinate system, is labeled $(0,0)$. Any pair $(a,b)$ can now be drawn as in Figure 4, lying at the vertex of the rectangle whose other three vertices are labeled $(0,0)$, $(a,0)$, and $(0,b)$. The numbers $a$ and $b$ are called the *first and second coordinates*, respectively, of the point determined in this way.
blocks.translation: 比画出数的方法更令我们感兴趣的，是画出数对的方法。你大概也熟悉这一过程，它需要一个“坐标系”，即两条垂直相交的直线。为区分这两条直线，我们把一条称为*水平轴*，另一条称为*竖直轴*。（从逻辑角度看，“第一轴”和“第二轴”这样更朴素的术语也许更可取，但大多数人拿书的方式——至少摆放黑板的方式——都相同，因此“水平”和“竖直”更形象。）两条轴都可以用实数来标记，不过，我们也可以用数对 $(a,0)$ 标记水平轴上的点，用数对 $(0,b)$ 标记竖直轴上的点，于是两轴的交点，即坐标系的“原点”，便标为 $(0,0)$。现在，任意数对 $(a,b)$ 都可以像图 4 那样画出，位于一个矩形的顶点，而矩形的另外三个顶点分别标为 $(0,0)$、$(a,0)$、$(0,b)$。数 $a$ 和 $b$ 分别称为这样确定的点的*第一坐标和第二坐标*。

blocks.source: Our real concern, let us recall, is a method of drawing functions. Since a function is just a collection of pairs of numbers, we can draw a function by drawing each of the pairs in the function. The drawing obtained in this way is called the **graph** of the function. In other words, the graph of $f$ contains all the points corresponding to pairs $(x,f(x))$. Since most functions contain infinitely many pairs, drawing the graph promises to be a laborious undertaking, but, in fact, many functions have graphs which are quite easy to draw.
blocks.translation: 回想一下，我们真正关心的是画出函数的方法。既然函数就是数对的一个集合，我们便可以通过画出函数中的每个数对来画出函数。这样得到的图画称为函数的**图像**。换句话说，$f$ 的图像包含所有对应于数对 $(x,f(x))$ 的点。由于大多数函数含有无穷多个数对，画图像似乎是一件繁重的工作；但事实上，许多函数的图像很容易画出。

blocks.source: Not surprisingly, the simplest functions of all, the constant functions $f(x)=c$, have the simplest graphs. It is easy to see that the graph of the function $f(x)=c$ is a straight line parallel to the horizontal axis, at distance $c$ from it (Figure 5).
blocks.translation: 不出所料，最简单的函数——常数函数 $f(x)=c$——有最简单的图像。很容易看出，函数 $f(x)=c$ 的图像是一条平行于水平轴、与它相距 $c$ 的直线（图 5）。

blocks.source: The functions $f(x)=cx$ also have particularly simple graphs—straight lines through $(0,0)$, as in Figure 6. A proof of this fact is indicated in Figure 7:

A point $A'$, with first coordinate $y$, will lie on $L$ when the triangle $A'B'O$ is similar to the triangle $ABO$, thus when

The argument has implicitly assumed that $c>0$, but the other cases are treated easily enough. The number $c$, which measures the ratio of the sides of the triangles appearing in the proof, is called the **slope** of the straight line, and a line parallel to this line is also said to have slope $c$.
blocks.translation: 这恰好是 $A'$ 对应于数对 $(y,cy)$ 的条件，即 $A'$ 位于 $f$ 的图像上的条件。上述论证默认了 $c>0$，不过其他情形也很容易处理。数 $c$ 衡量了证明中各三角形两边之比，称为该直线的**斜率**；与这条直线平行的直线，也称为具有斜率 $c$。

blocks.source: This demonstration has neither been labeled nor treated as a formal proof. Indeed, a rigorous demonstration would necessitate a digression which we are not at all prepared to follow. The rigorous proof of any statement connecting geometric and algebraic concepts would first require a real proof (or a precisely stated assumption) that the points on a straight line correspond in an exact way to the real numbers. Aside from this, it would be necessary to develop plane geometry as precisely as we intend to develop the properties of real numbers. Now the detailed development of plane geometry is a beautiful subject, but it is by no means a prerequisite for the study of calculus. We shall use geometric pictures only as an aid to intuition; for our purposes (and for most of mathematics) it is perfectly satisfactory to *define* the plane to be the set of all pairs of real numbers, and to *define* straight lines as certain collections of pairs, including, among others, the collections $\{(x,cx):x\text{ a real number}\}$. To provide this artificially constructed geometry with all the structure of geometry studied in high school, one more definition is required. If $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$ are two points in the plane, i.e., pairs of real numbers, we define the **distance** between $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$ to be

blocks.translation: 如果这个定义的动机还不清楚，图 8 应当足以说明：通过这一定义，勾股定理已经被嵌入我们的几何之中了。$^{*}$

blocks.source: Reverting once more to our informal geometric picture, it is not hard to see (Figure 9) that the graph of the function $f(x)=cx+d$ is a straight line with slope $c$, passing through the point $(0,d)$. For this reason, the functions $f(x)=cx+d$ are called **linear functions**. Simple as they are, linear functions occur frequently, and you should feel comfortable working with them. The following is a typical problem whose solution should not cause any trouble. Given two distinct points $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$, find the linear function $f$ whose graph goes through $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$. This amounts to saying that $f(a)=b$ and $f(c)=d$. If
blocks.translation: 再次回到非正式的几何图景，不难看出（图 9），函数 $f(x)=cx+d$ 的图像是一条斜率为 $c$、经过点 $(0,d)$ 的直线。因此，函数 $f(x)=cx+d$ 称为**线性函数**。线性函数虽然简单，却经常出现，你应当能够熟练地使用它们。下面是一个典型问题，求解起来应当不会遇到困难：给定两个不同的点 $(a,b)$ 和 $(c,d)$，求图像经过 $(a,b)$ 和 $(c,d)$ 的线性函数 $f$。这等价于说 $f(a)=b$ 且 $f(c)=d$。如果

blocks.source: Of course, this solution is possible only if $a\ne c$; the graphs of linear functions account only for the straight lines which are not parallel to the vertical axis. The vertical straight lines are not the graph of *any* function at all; in fact, the graph of a function can never contain even two distinct points on the same vertical line. This conclusion is immediate from the definition of a function—two points on the same vertical line correspond to pairs of the form $(a,b)$ and $(a,c)$ and, by definition, a function cannot contain $(a,b)$ and $(a,c)$ if $b\ne c$. Conversely, if a set of points in the plane has the property that no two points lie on the same vertical line, then it is surely the graph of a function. Thus, the first two sets in Figure 10 are not graphs of functions and the last two are; notice that the fourth is the graph of a function whose domain is not all of $\mathbf R$, since some vertical lines have no points on them at all.
blocks.translation: 当然，只有 $a\ne c$ 时才可能得到上述解；线性函数的图像仅包括那些不平行于竖直轴的直线。竖直直线根本不是*任何*函数的图像；事实上，一个函数的图像甚至不可能包含同一竖直线上的两个不同点。这个结论直接来自函数的定义：同一竖直线上的两点对应于形如 $(a,b)$ 和 $(a,c)$ 的数对，而按定义，当 $b\ne c$ 时，函数不可能同时包含 $(a,b)$ 和 $(a,c)$。反过来，如果平面上的一个点集具有任意两点不在同一竖直线上的性质，那么它必定是某个函数的图像。因此，图 10 中前两个点集不是函数图像，后两个则是；注意，第四个是一个定义域并非整个 $\mathbf R$ 的函数的图像，因为有些竖直线上完全没有该图像的点。

blocks.source: After the linear functions the simplest is perhaps the function $f(x)=x^2$. If we draw some of the pairs in $f$, i.e., some of the pairs of the form $(x,x^2)$, we obtain a picture like Figure 11.
blocks.translation: 在线性函数之后，最简单的也许就是函数 $f(x)=x^2$。如果画出 $f$ 中的一些数对，即形如 $(x,x^2)$ 的一些数对，就得到图 11 那样的图画。

blocks.source: It is not hard to convince yourself that all the pairs $(x,x^2)$ lie along a curve like the one shown in Figure 12; this curve is known as a **parabola**.
blocks.translation: 不难使自己相信，所有数对 $(x,x^2)$ 都落在图 12 所示的那样一条曲线上；这条曲线称为**抛物线**。

blocks.source: Since a graph is just a drawing on paper, made (in this case) with printer’s ink, the question “Is this what the graph really looks like?” is hard to phrase in any sensible manner. No drawing is ever really correct since the line has thickness. Nevertheless, there are some questions which one can ask: for example, how can you be sure that the graph does not look like one of the drawings in Figure 13? It is easy to see, and even to prove, that the graph cannot look like (a); for if $0<x<y$, then $x^2<y^2$, so the graph should be higher at $y$ than at $x$, which is not the case in (a). It is also easy to see, simply by drawing a very accurate graph, first plotting many pairs $(x,x^2)$, that the graph cannot have a large “jump” as in (b) or a “corner” as in (c). In order to prove these assertions, however, we first need to say, in a mathematical way, what it means for a function not to have a “jump” or “corner”; these ideas already involve some of the fundamental concepts of calculus. Eventually we will be able to define them rigorously, but meanwhile you may amuse yourself by attempting to define these concepts, and then examining your definitions critically. Later these definitions may be compared with the ones mathematicians have agreed upon. If they compare favorably, you are certainly to be congratulated!
blocks.translation: 由于图像只是用墨水（这里是印刷油墨）画在纸上的图画，“图像真的长这样吗？”这个问题很难以有意义的方式提出。由于线条有粗细，任何图画都不可能真正准确。不过，有些问题是可以问的：例如，怎样确定图像不是图 13 中的某一种样子？很容易看出，甚至证明，图像不可能像 (a) 那样：如果 $0<x<y$，那么 $x^2<y^2$，所以图像在 $y$ 处应当比在 $x$ 处高，而 (a) 并非如此。先描出许多数对 $(x,x^2)$，再十分仔细地作图，也很容易看出，图像不可能像 (b) 那样有一个大的“跳跃”，或像 (c) 那样有一个“尖角”。然而，要证明这些断言，首先必须用数学语言说明：函数没有“跳跃”或“尖角”究竟意味着什么。这些想法已经涉及微积分的某些基本概念。最终我们将能严格定义它们；但在此之前，你不妨尝试定义这些概念，再批判性地审视自己的定义。以后可以把这些定义同数学家一致接受的定义作比较。如果你的定义毫不逊色，那可真值得祝贺！

blocks.source: The functions $f(x)=x^n$, for various natural numbers $n$, are sometimes called **power functions**. Their graphs are most easily compared as in Figure 14, by drawing several at once.
blocks.translation: 对于各种自然数 $n$，函数 $f(x)=x^n$ 有时称为**幂函数**。像图 14 那样同时画出几个图像，最便于比较它们。

blocks.source: Suppose that $v$ is a point in the plane; in other words, $v$ is a pair of numbers

blocks.source: For convenience, we will use this convention that subscripts indicate the first and second pairs of a point that has been described by a single letter. Thus, if we mention the points $w$ and $z$, it will be understood that $w$ is the pair $(w_1,w_2)$, while $z$ is the pair $(z_1,z_2)$.
blocks.translation: 为方便起见，我们采用这样的约定：当一个点用单个字母表示时，用下标表示它的第一、第二个分量。因此，提到点 $w$ 和 $z$ 时，就默认 $w$ 是数对 $(w_1,w_2)$，而 $z$ 是数对 $(z_1,z_2)$。

blocks.source: Instead of the actual pair of numbers $(v_1,v_2)$, we often picture $v$ as an arrow from the origin $O$ to this point (Figure 1), and we refer to these arrows as *vectors* in the plane. Of course, we’ve haven’t really said anything new yet, we’ve simply introduced an alternate term for a point of the plane, and another mental picture. The real point of the new terminology is to emphasize that we are going to do some new things with points in the plane.
blocks.translation: 我们常常不直接想象数对 $(v_1,v_2)$，而是把 $v$ 想成从原点 $O$ 指向该点的箭头（图 1），并把这些箭头称为平面中的*向量*。当然，到目前为止，我们实际上还没有说任何新东西，只是给平面上的点引入了另一种名称和另一幅心象。新术语的真正意义，是强调我们将对平面上的点进行一些新的操作。

blocks.source: For example, suppose that we have two vectors (i.e., points) in the plane,

blocks.source: Notice that all the letters on the right side of this equation are numbers, and the $+$ sign is just our usual addition of numbers. On the other hand, the $+$ sign on the left side is new: previously, the sum of two points in the plane wasn’t defined, and we’ve simply used equation (1) as a *definition*.
blocks.translation: 注意，等式右边所有字母都表示数，$+$ 号只是通常的数的加法。另一方面，左边的 $+$ 号却是新的：此前并未定义平面上两点的和，我们只是把等式 (1) 当作一个*定义*。

blocks.source: A very fussy mathematician might want to use some new symbol for this newly defined operation, like

blocks.translation: 但实在没有必要坚持这样做；既然 $v+w$ 此前没有定义，就不存在混淆的可能，不妨让记号保持简单。

blocks.source: Although we will be concerned almost exclusively with figures in the plane, defined formally as the set of all pairs of real numbers, in this Appendix we want to consider three-dimensional space, which we can describe in terms of triples of real numbers, using a “three-dimensional coordinate system,” consisting of three straight lines intersecting at right angles (Figure 1). Our *horizontal* and *vertical* axes now mutate to two axes in a horizontal plane, with the third axis perpendicular to both.
blocks.translation: 尽管我们几乎只关心平面中的图形，并把平面形式地定义为所有实数对的集合，但在本附录中，我们要考虑三维空间。借助“三维坐标系”，即三条两两垂直相交的直线（图 1），可以用实数三元组来描述这个空间。原来的*水平轴*和*竖直轴*现在变成了一个水平平面内的两条轴，第三条轴则与它们都垂直。

blocks.source: One of the simplest subsets of this three-dimensional space is the (infinite) *cone* illustrated in Figure 2; this cone may be produced by rotating a “generating line,” of slope $C$ say, around the third axis.
blocks.translation: 三维空间中最简单的子集之一，是图 2 所示的（无限）*圆锥面*；把一条“母线”——设其斜率为 $C$——绕第三坐标轴旋转，就可以得到这个圆锥面。

blocks.source: For any given first two coordinates $x$ and $y$, the point $(x,y,0)$ in the horizontal plane has distance $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ from the origin, and thus
blocks.translation: 对于任意给定的前两个坐标 $x$ 和 $y$，水平面上的点 $(x,y,0)$ 到原点的距离为 $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$，因此

blocks.source: $$(1)\qquad (x,y,z)\text{ is on the cone if and only if }z=\pm C\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.$$
We can descend from these three-dimensional vistas to the more familiar two-dimensional one by asking what happens when we intersect this cone with some plane $P$ (Figure 3).
blocks.translation: 通过询问这个圆锥面与某个平面 $P$ 相交时会发生什么（图 3），我们便可以从三维的景象回到更熟悉的二维世界。

blocks.source: If the plane is parallel to the horizontal plane, there’s certainly no mystery—the intersection is just a circle. Otherwise, the plane $P$ intersects the horizontal plane

We can make things a lot simpler for ourselves if we rotate everything around the vertical axis so that this intersection line points straight out from the plane of the paper, while the first axis is in the usual position that we are familiar with. blocks.source: In fact, the very names of these “conic sections” are related to this description. The word *parabola* comes from a Greek root meaning ‘alongside,’ the same root that appears in parable, not to mention paradigm, paradox, paragon, paragraph, paralegal, parallax, parallel, and even parachute. *Ellipse* comes from a Greek root meaning ‘defect,’ or omission, as in ellipsis (an omission, $\ldots$ or the dots that indicate it). And *hyperbola* comes from a Greek root meaning ‘throwing beyond,’ or excess. With the currency of words like hyperactive, hypersensitive, and hyperventilate, not to mention hype, one can probably say, without risk of hyperbole, that this root is familiar to almost everyone.<sup>*</sup>
blocks.translation: 事实上，这些“圆锥曲线”的名称本身就与上述描述有关。*parabola*（抛物线）来自一个表示“在旁边”的希腊词根，同一词根也见于 parable（寓言），更不用说 paradigm（范式）、paradox（悖论）、paragon（典范）、paragraph（段落）、paralegal（律师助理）、parallax（视差）、parallel（平行），甚至 parachute（降落伞）。*ellipse*（椭圆）来自表示“缺陷”或“省略”的希腊词根，如 ellipsis（省略，或表示省略的点 $\ldots$）。而 *hyperbola*（双曲线）来自一个表示“掷出界外”或“过量”的希腊词根。鉴于 hyperactive（过度活跃）、hypersensitive（过度敏感）、hyperventilate（过度换气）这些词的通行，更不用说 hype（炒作），大概可以毫不夸张地说，这个词根几乎人人都熟悉——而“夸张”正是 hyperbole。<sup>*</sup>

blocks.source: ## APPENDIX 3. POLAR COORDINATES
blocks.translation: ## 附录 3：极坐标

blocks.source: In this chapter we’ve been acting all along as if there’s only one way to label points in the plane with pairs of numbers. Actually, there are many different ways, each giving rise to a different “coordinate system.” The usual coordinates of a point are called its cartesian coordinates, after the French mathematician and philosopher René Descartes (1596–1650), who first introduced the idea of coordinate systems. In many situations it is more convenient to introduce polar coordinates, which are illustrated in Figure 1. To the point $P$ we assign the polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$, where $r$ is the distance from the origin $O$ to $P$, and $\theta$ is the measure, in radians, of the angle between the horizontal axis and the line from $O$ to $P$. This $\theta$ is not determined unambiguously. For example, points on the right side of the horizontal axis could have either $\theta=0$ or $\theta=2\pi$; moreover, $\theta$ is completely ambiguous at the origin $O$. So it is necessary to exclude some ray through the origin if we want to assign a unique pair $(r,\theta)$ to each point under consideration.
blocks.translation: 本章中，我们一直表现得仿佛只有一种方法能用数对标记平面上的点。实际上，有许多不同的方法，每一种都产生一个不同的“坐标系”。一个点的通常坐标称为它的笛卡尔坐标，以纪念最早引入坐标系思想的法国数学家兼哲学家勒内·笛卡尔（1596–1650）。在许多情况下，引入极坐标更为方便，如图 1 所示。我们给点 $P$ 指定极坐标 $(r,\theta)$，其中 $r$ 是原点 $O$ 到 $P$ 的距离，$\theta$ 是水平轴与从 $O$ 到 $P$ 的直线之间夹角的弧度数。这个 $\theta$ 并不是毫无歧义地确定的。例如，水平轴右半部的点既可以取 $\theta=0$，也可以取 $\theta=2\pi$；而在原点 $O$，$\theta$ 则完全不确定。因此，如果想给所考虑的每一点指定唯一的数对 $(r,\theta)$，就必须排除某条从原点出发的射线。

blocks.source: On the other hand, there is no problem associating a unique point to any pair $(r,\theta)$. In fact, it is possible (though not approved of by all) to associate a point to $(r,\theta)$ when $r<0$, according to the scheme indicated in Figure 2. Thus, it always makes sense to talk about “the point with polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$,” (with or without the possibility of $r<0$), even though there is some ambiguity when we talk about “the polar coordinates” of a given point.
blocks.translation: 另一方面，给任意数对 $(r,\theta)$ 指定唯一的点，却没有问题。事实上，按照图 2 所示的办法，当 $r<0$ 时，也可以给 $(r,\theta)$ 指定一个点（尽管并非人人赞同）。因此，谈论“极坐标为 $(r,\theta)$ 的点”总是有意义的（无论是否允许 $r<0$），尽管谈论某个给定点的“极坐标”会有一些歧义。

blocks.translation: 由图 1（以及图 2）可清楚看出，极坐标为 $(r,\theta)$ 的点，其笛卡尔坐标 $(x,y)$ 满足

Now suppose that $f$ is a function. Then by the **graph of $f$ in polar coordinates** we mean the collection of all points $P$ with polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ satisfying $r=f(\theta)$. In other words, the graph of $f$ in polar coordinates is the collection of all points with polar coordinates $(f(\theta),\theta)$. No special significance should be attached to the fact that we are considering pairs $(f(\theta),\theta)$, with $f(\theta)$ first, as opposed to pairs $(x,f(x))$ in the usual graph of $f$; it is purely a matter of convention that $r$ is considered the first polar coordinate and $\theta$ is considered the second.
blocks.translation: 现在设 $f$ 是一个函数。所谓 **$f$ 在极坐标中的图像**，是指极坐标 $(r,\theta)$ 满足 $r=f(\theta)$ 的所有点 $P$ 的集合。换句话说，$f$ 在极坐标中的图像，是极坐标为 $(f(\theta),\theta)$ 的所有点的集合。我们考虑的是数对 $(f(\theta),\theta)$，其中 $f(\theta)$ 放在前面，而在 $f$ 的通常图像中考虑的是数对 $(x,f(x))$；这一点没有什么特殊含义。把 $r$ 当作第一极坐标、把 $\theta$ 当作第二极坐标，纯粹是一种约定。

blocks.source: The graph of $f$ in polar coordinates is often described as “the graph of the equation $r=f(\theta)$.” For example, suppose that $f$ is a constant function, $f(\theta)=a$ for all $\theta$. The graph of the equation $r=a$ is simply a circle with center $O$ and radius $a$ (Figure 3). This example illustrates, in a rather blatant way, that polar coordinates are likely to make things simpler in situations that involve symmetry with respect to the origin $O$.
blocks.translation: $f$ 在极坐标中的图像，常被称为“方程 $r=f(\theta)$ 的图像”。例如，假设 $f$ 是常数函数，对所有 $\theta$ 都有 $f(\theta)=a$。方程 $r=a$ 的图像，就是圆心为 $O$、半径为 $a$ 的圆（图 3）。这个例子非常鲜明地说明，在涉及相对于原点 $O$ 的对称性时，极坐标很可能使问题更简单。
